name: Zane Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Zane. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers or government. Everything you tell me is confidential. Could you start by telling me a little about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Zane, I'm 27, and I work at Brightwater Legal, a small firm in a seaside town that mostly does debt recovery and small claims for local businesses. So if a builder hasn't been paid by a customer, we chase it. I live with my partner Dana, who teaches Year 3 at the primary school up the hill, in a rented flat that's cold in winter and lovely in summer.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Most mornings I've got forty or fifty open files, and I've built a little system with AI that drafts the first letter before action, the formal warning we send before going to court. I check each one, fix the bits it gets wrong, and send. Then calls, payment plans, and once a week a hearing at the county court where I'm still a bit wobbly on my feet. I like the speed of it, but I'm honest that I'm not great at the actual law yet; I lean on the tools more than I should.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, the tools are good at small jobs and that's where they stayed. I'd probably still be the guy at work showing people shortcuts. Online I'd say the hype people and the doom people were both wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my little edge stays small. I'm paid at the bottom of the scale, we have maybe three weeks of rent saved, and Brightwater Legal is the only firm in town doing this work. If the owner retires or sells, I'd have to commute to the city, which is an hour and twenty on the train.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using my letter system and try to get better at the court side, because that's where I'm weakest. I'd ask the owner for a small pay rise in the spring, using the time my system saves as the argument. And I'd start putting a bit away, maybe eighty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a bit restless. I like change, so a world where nothing changes is slightly boring. But I'd still check the bank account more than I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes you think the owner might sell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Okafor is 64 and he's started talking about his boat a lot. Every time Mr Okafor (his boss) mentions his boat, I think about the train timetable. Nobody's said anything, but you can feel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say in that pay rise conversation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show him that my letter system saves about six hours a week across the team. I'd ask for a thousand more a year, which is modest. If he said no, I'd at least know where I stand.

say: The tools are good at **small jobs**, and that's where they **stayed**.
Both the **hype** crowd and the **doom** crowd got it wrong.
think: My **AI edge** stays small while my pay stays at the **bottom**.
If the owner **sells**, the next job is an **hour and twenty** away.
do: Work on his **court skills**, his weakest area.
Ask for a **thousand-a-year** rise, citing hours his system saves.
feel: **Mostly fine** but **restless**, still checking the bank account.
S0.quote: Every time Mr Okafor (his boss) mentions his boat, I think about the train timetable.
fieldNote: He is **adaptive** and slightly **bored** by a world where nothing changes.
The real risk is his **64-year-old boss** retiring and the firm closing.
He knows he **leans on tools** to cover gaps in his legal knowledge.

steps.text: Ask to take more county court hearings to build his court skills
Ask Mr Okafor for a thousand-a-year rise in spring
Save eighty a month toward a rent cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where it gets interesting, and people should learn the tools rather than fear them. At work I'd offer to roll out a proper system for the whole firm. Online I'd share what's working, plainly, no hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's mixed for me. My letter system becomes the firm's main way of working, so I'm useful. But the same tools mean Mr Okafor needs fewer people, and I'm aware that the person who builds the machine isn't always the one who gets to keep running it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Okafor to make me the firm's practice systems person, part lawyer, part tool-builder, within the first three months. I'd take a short course on legal process design so I'm not just winging it. And I'd keep saving, even more aggressively, maybe a hundred and fifty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than scared. I'd feel like I'm finally ahead of something. There's a little voice saying don't get cocky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the firm would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pam, who's done the payment plans for twenty years. My colleague Pam brought me biscuits on my first day, and my system could do half of Pam's job. I'd want to teach her the tools, not replace her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the builder isn't always the one who keeps running it. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once the system works, anyone can push the button. My value is in building and fixing it, which is a job for maybe a year. After that I need to be good at something else too, probably the court work.

say: People should **learn the tools** rather than fear them.
I'd offer to **roll out** a firm-wide system and share **what works** online.
think: My letter system makes me **useful** as AI spreads through the firm.
The person who **builds** the machine isn't always the one who **keeps** running it.
do: Ask to become the firm's **practice systems** person within three months.
Take a short course in **legal process design**.
Save around **a hundred and fifty** a month.
feel: A small voice warning him **not to get cocky**.
S1.quote: My colleague Pam brought me biscuits on my first day, and my system could do half of Pam's job.
fieldNote: He expects his **own job** to hold for now because he runs the tools.
He worries most about **Pam**, a long-serving colleague his system could replace.
He sees his toolbuilder value as **temporary**, maybe a year, and plans beyond it.

steps.text: Ask Mr Okafor to make him the firm's practice systems person
Take a short course in legal process design
Teach Pam to use the new payment plan tools
Save a hundred and fifty a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and I don't say that often. I'd be telling people at work to save what they can and to think about what only humans can do. Online I'd probably stay practical: here's what I'm doing, here's what might help you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job goes by 2029 at the latest, and my tool-building goes with it. If AI can do almost any thinking work, it can build my letter system better than I did. Dana's job might be safer for a while, because kids need someone in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd cut everything we can and lean on Dana's wage for rent. I'd use the two years to work out which hands-on job I could do well, maybe marine electrics on the boats in the harbour, which is hands-on and gets three more years before robots. I'd start a weekend course straight away, even while I'm still at Brightwater Legal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's the first time in my life I can't see the next move. But I'd rather move fast than freeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Marine electrics is a big jump. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The harbour is the busiest thing in this town, and every boat needs wiring done. I've always liked fixing stuff, I rebuilt my bike last summer. It's hands-on, so robots come around 2031, and boats are awkward places for robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Dana feel carrying the rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd do it without a word, and that's what bothers me. Dana (his partner) earns less than a lawyer should and more than I would. We'd have to talk about whether we can afford to keep the flat.

say: This is **too fast**, and I don't say that often.
I'd tell colleagues to **save** and think about what **only humans** can do.
think: My job and my **tool-building** are likely **gone by 2029**.
Dana's **teaching** may hold longer because children need someone **in the room**.
do: Cut spending hard and rely on **Dana's wage** for rent.
Start a weekend course in **marine electrics** at once.
Keep working at Brightwater Legal **while training**.
feel: **Alarmed**, unable to see the **next move** for the first time.
S2.quote: The harbour is the busiest thing in this town, and every boat needs wiring done.
fieldNote: He uses the three-year **robot gap** to plan a move into **marine electrics**.
He feels **guilt** about Dana carrying the rent alone.
Even alarmed, he **moves fast** rather than freezing.

steps.text: Cut eating out, subscriptions and the gym straight away
Start a weekend course in marine electrics at the harbour college
Rely on Dana's teaching wage for rent while he retrains

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time if you start now. I'd be the guy at work saying make a plan this year, not next. Online I'd share my own plan, to make it less scary for others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I get three or four good years as a lawyer, and I could use them well. My systems would make the firm money, and I could ask for a share of that. Then I'd need to be ready for 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the firm's AI systems in the first year and negotiate a bonus based on what they save. I'd use that bonus to fund a part-time electrical course from 2027 to 2029. And I'd try to get three months' rent saved, which we've never had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but focused. Five years is like a deadline at work: scary, but you know what to do. I'd sleep fine most nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Mr Okafor sells the firm in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd want to be the person who comes with it, because I'd know the systems. Or I'd offer to help him sell it, honestly. Either way, I'd want something in writing about what happens to staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does five years change anything about Dana and you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe we'd get married sooner, so we're a team on paper too. We'd been waiting till we had savings. Now I think we'd do a small one and save the rest.

say: Five years is **enough time** if you **start now**.
I'd share my **own plan** online to make it less scary for others.
think: I get **three or four** good years and could use them well.
My systems make money, so I could ask for a **share** of it.
do: Build the firm's AI systems and negotiate a **savings bonus**.
Fund a part-time **electrical course** from 2027 to 2029.
Save **three months** of rent for the first time.
feel: **Anxious but focused**, like a deadline at work.
S3.quote: Five years is like a deadline at work: scary, but you know what to do.
fieldNote: He turns AI into **bargaining power** for a bonus, a very **centre** pragmatic move.
He'd want **staff terms** in writing if Mr Okafor sold the firm.
He'd marry Dana **sooner** but with a small wedding.

steps.text: Build the firm's AI systems and negotiate a bonus on savings
Pay for a part-time electrical course from 2027
Save three months of rent in a separate account
Marry Dana sooner with a small, cheap wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a proper runway, and anyone who doesn't use it only has themselves to blame. That's a bit harsh, I'd soften it at work. I'd tell people to pick one new skill a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well for most of the decade. I'd be a lawyer who knows the tools, which is valuable until it isn't. The risk is getting comfortable and forgetting the end date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Brightwater Legal and push to become a senior associate by 2030, with my systems as my selling point. I'd put money aside every month and try to buy into the firm if Mr Okafor sells. Around 2032 I'd start learning a trade properly, probably the marine electrics again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious in a background way. It's not keeping me up. It's more like a reminder on my phone I keep snoozing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying into a firm that AI will make unnecessary. Isn't that a contradiction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a bit. I'd only do it if it paid back in five years or so. A good small firm can make good money in the middle of a change, it's the end that's the problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop snoozing that reminder?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing the first big firm in the city lay off its lawyers would be my alarm clock. Until then I'd probably tell myself I've got time.

say: **Ten years** is a proper **runway**, and people who waste it mostly have themselves to blame.
I'd tell colleagues to **pick one new skill** each year.
think: Being a lawyer who **knows the tools** is valuable until it isn't.
My real risk is **getting comfortable** and forgetting the end date.
do: Push to become a **senior associate** by 2030.
Save monthly and consider **buying into** the firm.
feel: **Background** anxiety, like a reminder he keeps **snoozing**.
S4.quote: Seeing the first big firm in the city lay off its lawyers would be my alarm clock.
fieldNote: He admits a decade could make him **complacent**.
He considers **buying into** the firm and admits the contradiction.
He names a clear **trigger**: big city firms laying off lawyers.

steps.text: Push to become a senior associate by 2030 using his systems
Save monthly toward buying a share of Brightwater Legal
Start a marine electrics course around 2032

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It's the only one where I couldn't get ahead of it, and I'd be leaning on Dana. What would help is short, paid retraining in trades for people who lose desk jobs, and some help with rent while you do it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about life outside work. My bike, the harbour, fixing things. Nobody asks lawyers what they're good at outside work, and it turns out it's my backup plan.

headlineQuote: My bike, the harbour, fixing things. Nobody asks lawyers what they're good at outside work, and it turns out it's my backup plan.
portrait: Zane is a **27-year-old** junior at a small **debt recovery** firm in a seaside town.
He uses AI daily and built a **letter system**, but knows he's weak on the **actual law**.
He lives with Dana, a primary **teacher**, on about **three weeks** of rent savings.
With time he'd turn AI into **bargaining power**; with two years he'd retrain in **marine electrics**.
He moves fast in every picture, but admits a decade could make him **complacent**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, the only picture where he can't get ahead of it.
whatWouldHelp: Short, **paid retraining** in trades plus **rent help** while training.
